newsitem.title: USA: Two Afghan diplomats wait to see who is in charge.
newsitem.headline: Two Afghan diplomats wait to see who is in charge.

text.p: Afghanistan's two diplomats in Washington shared an embassy office on Thursday, while the State Department mulled which one of them should be the official representative.

Both charge d'affaires Yar Mohammad Mohabbat and second secretary Seraj Jamal stressed that business was proceeding as usual, despite the fact that Jamal maintained that he -- and not his immediate boss -- had the support of Afghanistan's Taleban rulers.
"We are working together right now...like friendly. This is politics, you know?" Jamal said by telephone.
Jamal said he was awaiting word from the State Department, which he said had received a letter from the Taleban in Kabul asking that he be in charge of Afghanistan's U.S. embassy.

A U.S. official confirmed that a diplomatic note from the Taleban was received. The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said of the Taleban proposal: "We're thinking about it but we haven't approved it."
The official also confirmed that Mohabbat had made a routine visit to the State Department to discuss, among other matters, staffing at the embassy.

Jamal and Mohabbat are the only two diplomats in the Washington diplomatic list for the Afghan embassy which until now has represented the government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani, ousted from Kabul by Taleban last September.
On Wednesday, Jamal took down the green, black and white flag of the former government and tried to raise the white flag of Taleban, a move that Mohabbat said was "not wise."
"This is like a coup in some countries," Mohabbat said in a separate telephone interview.
Mohabbat confirmed that the two were sharing an office, and said the old government flag was currently flying outside the embassy.

Because of the civil war in Afghanistan, the United States has maintained no diplomats in Kabul since the late 1980s and conducts its relations with the various Afghan factions through its embassy in Pakistan.

Taleban strengthened its claim to be the government of Afghanistan when it seized territory held by a rival group in the north of the country last weekend, although it lost control on Wednesday of the key city of Mazar-i-Sharif.
The United States has evaded the issue of whether it is recognising a Taleban government by saying it recognises states, not governments.
